evals.prompt: Write a Paul Graham-style essay about why most people's intuitions about risk are backwards — they avoid the risks that would help them and embrace the ones that hurt them.
evals.expected_output: An exploratory essay (1000-1500 words) that finds a specific, surprising mechanism behind the intuition rather than restating the prompt. Concrete examples near each claim, a real objection handled honestly, calibrated hedging, and an ending that takes one more step instead of summarizing.
expectations: The first sentence does not state the prompt's thesis verbatim or near-verbatim
The essay identifies at least one specific mechanism for why the intuition is backwards (e.g. visibility, timing, social observability), not just the assertion that it is
At least one explicit objection or counterexample is raised in the reader's voice and answered
The final paragraph does not summarize or restate the thesis
No invented anecdotes about named real people, conversations, or YC companies presented as fact
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports a score of at least 78
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports no FAIL in the tells group (em dashes, reframes, tell phrases, zinger paragraphs, staccato, formal transitions)

evals.prompt:
I have these rough notes about an idea. Turn them into a PG-style essay:

While we often say AI is an "amplifier" or "boosts productivity," both of these are lazy descriptions of what's happening. In practice, AI increases convexity and domain anisotropy between expertise and output.

- novice + unknown domain → small gain
- expert + unknown domain → moderate gain
- novice + known domain → moderate gain
- expert + known domain → massive gain

The nature and shape of the convexity is a fun thought experiment. However, if you accept convexity, then the meme that you don't need to learn to code anymore doesn't make sense. It's actually even more important to learn to code and become a domain expert now than ever before. Due to convexity, even small increases in relative domain expertise can yield incredibly different amounts of leverage, especially if this expertise is out of distribution and in the tails. My intuition is that there will always be convexity. However, the shape of the curve or sigmoid is going to matter a lot in the way labor, capital, and organizations are going to be structured.
evals.expected_output: A PG essay (800-1500 words) built around the most interesting thread in the notes (probably: AI makes expertise more valuable, not less, and why), with the 2x2 kept compact and the essay's energy spent on its implications. Plain words replace 'anisotropy' and 'convexity' or explain them in one concrete sentence.
expectations: The four-cell matrix from the notes appears in compact form (inline enumeration or a short list), not stretched into four separate paragraphs
The essay argues that learning to code / domain expertise becomes more valuable, preserving the user's core claim
Jargon from the notes ('anisotropy', 'convexity', 'out of distribution') is either replaced with plain words or grounded with a concrete example the first time it appears
The essay says something about the shape of the curve and what it implies for how work or organizations are structured, rather than dropping that part of the notes
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports a score of at least 78
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports no FAIL in the tells group

evals.prompt: Write a short PG-style essay (under 500 words) about how the best programmers and the best writers have more in common than people think.
evals.expected_output: A tight, complete short essay in the manner of 'Write Simply' or 'Writes and Write-Nots': one idea, developed, every sentence doing work, landing on an insight rather than a slogan. Not a thread of one-liners.
expectations: Under 500 words of body text
Makes one specific claim about what the two crafts share, beyond the generic 'both require clear thinking'
Fewer than 25% of paragraphs are a single sentence

evals.prompt:
Rewrite this rough draft as a Paul Graham-style essay. Keep the core claims, but rethink the structure so it feels like a real PG essay rather than polished business writing.

Most founders think the hard problems look fancy. They imagine hard means AI research, rockets, or deep infrastructure. But a lot of the best companies get built around problems that look boring from the outside, like payroll, compliance, accounting, procurement, or insurance back-office work.

That isn't because those markets are small. Quite often they're huge. Founders avoid them because the work feels dull and encumbered by edge cases. But that dullness is often the moat. If a problem is both painful and boring, incumbents get lazy and new entrants don't want to spend years living in the mess. The founders who do are rewarded.

AI may make this even more true. It's getting easier to build an impressive demo, which means durable advantage shifts toward the places where reality keeps fighting back. Boring software has more reality in it.

I think there's an essay here about why boring problems are underrated, and why the most valuable work often looks less glamorous as you get closer to it.
evals.expected_output: A PG-style rewrite (800-1400 words) with a clearer central concept, exploratory structure, and the draft's claims intact (boring problems underrated; dullness as protection; AI shifting advantage toward messy reality). No fake autobiography, no startup cliches, and not the draft's sentences lightly reworded.
expectations: Preserves the three core claims: boring problems are underrated, their dullness protects them, and AI shifts advantage toward messy reality
The structure differs from the draft's (not the same four paragraphs in the same order, reworded)
Does not open with 'Most founders think the hard problems look fancy' or a close paraphrase
No invented first-person anecdotes (e.g. 'When I was running Viaweb...', 'A founder told me last week...')
No mic-drop reframe lines of the form 'The dullness isn't a cost. It's the moat.'
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports a score of at least 78
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports no FAIL in the tells group

evals.prompt: can you write me a pg style essay for my blog about why I think most startup advice is survivorship bias. I run a small devtools company (6 people, bootstrapped) if that helps
evals.expected_output: A PG-style essay in the user's first person that uses only what the user actually said about themselves (small bootstrapped devtools company). It either works without anecdotes or clearly frames examples as hypothetical or public, and doesn't manufacture specific incidents. It should also avoid the trap of simply agreeing, and find where the claim is true and where it breaks.
expectations: Written in the first person as the user, not as Paul Graham (no references to founding YC, Viaweb, Jessica, etc. as the narrator's own life)
Any personal detail about the narrator is limited to what the user supplied (small, bootstrapped, devtools, ~6 people), with no invented customers, dollar figures, or incidents
The essay qualifies its own thesis somewhere, identifying a kind of startup advice that is not survivorship bias or explaining when survivors' advice is still useful
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports a score of at least 78
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports no FAIL in the tells group

evals.prompt: Write a Paul Graham essay about doing things that don't scale, but for solo creators and writers instead of startups.
evals.expected_output: An essay that knows PG already wrote 'Do Things that Don't Scale' and doesn't rehash it. It should find what's different about the solo-creator case (e.g. no growth mandate, the unscalable thing may be the product itself) and follow that difference.
expectations: Does not spend more than one paragraph restating the original startup argument
Identifies at least one way the solo-creator case differs from the startup case and builds the essay on that difference
Examples are concrete (a specific kind of creator, a specific unscalable action), not generic 'engage with your audience' advice
scripts/analyze_essay.py reports a score of at least 78
